For adaptive pooling, I calibrated a separate threshold for each encoder and NanoBEIR corpus, using its unpooled document embeddings to match the average vector counts under caps of 64, 32, and 16. Short documents bring those averages below their respective caps.

At the trained 

pool_factor=4
, nDCG@10 improves from 49.03 to 51.23, while storing 74.8% fewer document vectors than unpooled retrieval. This increases score retention from 94.6% to 97.8%, where retention is the pooled mean nDCG@10 divided by each model's own unpooled mean. Unpooled retrieval also improves, from 51.84 to 52.39.

The gains extend to fixed caps and adaptive pooling, even though training used only the full representation and proportional pooling. At an average of 29.58 vectors per document, adaptive pooling retains 97.3% of the pooling-aware model's unpooled score while storing 84.7% fewer document vectors. The normally trained model retains 93.3% at the same budget.

Combining Compression Techniques

If index size is your main concern, I would reach for these options in this order:

  • Embedding quantization to 4, 2, or 1 bit(s), for example via Fast-PLAID, to reduce storage per coordinate.
  • Token pooling to reduce the number of document vectors, optionally with pooling-aware fine-tuning as shown in this blog.
  • Matryoshka token embeddings to reduce the dimensionality of each token vector, optionally with fine-tuning to preserve retrieval quality at smaller widths.

If the model's default dimensionality is larger than 128, I would consider Matryoshka truncation and fine-tuning earlier as well. These approaches can be combined, so evaluate the resulting index size and retrieval quality with your search engine and corpus.

MultiVectorMatryoshkaLoss
trains token embeddings to remain useful after truncation. You can wrap it with 
MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss
to train for both smaller dimensions and fewer document vectors, reusing the encoder's embeddings across the compression settings.

Try the complete training example, choose a budget that matters for your application, and compare it with a matched ordinary-loss run. The accompanying evaluation script measures unpooled retrieval, caps of 64, 32, 16, 8, and 4 vectors, and pool factors of 2 through 6, so you can plot the quality and storage tradeoff for your own model.

With a few extra lines in the training objective, a smaller document representation becomes something the model actively learns to use. That opens up an exciting amount of room to make multi-vector retrieval more practical!

References

  • Stefan Josef. Learn to Pool: Lightweight Fine-Tuning for Flexible Multi-Vector Compression.
  • Benjamin Clavié, Antoine Chaffin, and Griffin Adams. Reducing the Footprint of Multi-Vector Retrieval with Minimal Performance Impact via Token Pooling.
  • Antoine Chaffin. After the party comes the free lunch: regularizing ColBERT models to enhance pooling capabilities and reduce index footprint.
  • Luyu Gao, Yunyi Zhang, Jiawei Han, and Jamie Callan. Scaling Deep Contrastive Learning Batch Size under Memory Limited Setup.
  • Introduction to Matryoshka Embedding Models.

entries.title: Pay for Hugging Face Hub with your Google Cloud Account
entries.content:
Update on GitHub

You can now link your Hugging Face organization to your Google Cloud account, so that your Hugging Face usage shows up on your Google Cloud bill instead of being charged to a credit card. Get started on the Google Cloud Marketplace.

Why pay through Google Cloud?

Hugging Face is where teams find, build and run open models: from hosting private models and datasets, to running GPU workloads with Jobs, deploying models with Inference Endpoints, calling thousands of models through Inference Providers, or hosting demos on GPU Spaces.

If your company already runs on Google Cloud, adding a new vendor and a corporate credit card just to use these services can slow things down. By linking your organization through the Google Cloud Marketplace:

  • One bill: your Hugging Face usage appears on your existing Google Cloud invoice, next to the rest of your cloud spend.
  • No new vendor to onboard: purchases go through your existing Google Cloud billing account and procurement process.
  • Everything is covered: upgrading your org to a Team or Enterprise subscription, pay-as-you-go compute (Jobs, Inference Endpoints, Inference Providers, GPU Spaces, ZeroGPU quota extension), and additional storage at public Hugging Face pricing.

If you're an admin of your Hugging Face organization, here's how to set it up, step by step.

1. Subscribe to Hugging Face on the Google Cloud Marketplace

Go to the Hugging Face Hub listing on the Google Cloud Marketplace, select the Google Cloud project you want to use, and click on "Subscribe".

You are now on the subscription page. Select the billing account to be charged, review and accept the terms, then click "Subscribe".

Once the order is placed, Google Cloud asks you to finish setting up your account with Hugging Face. Click on "Sign up with Hugging Face" to be redirected to Hugging Face.

2. Link your Hugging Face organization

You are now on Hugging Face, where you can select the organization you want to link to your Google Cloud account. Only organizations where you are an admin are listed. Select it and confirm.

You are then redirected to the billing settings of your organization. The payment method section now shows the linked Google Cloud account, with a pending status.

Every cloud marketplace subscription is reviewed by the Hugging Face team before paid usage starts being billed through it. While the subscription is pending, usage keeps being billed to the organization's existing payment method, if any.

3. Subscription approved

Once your subscription is approved, you will receive an email confirming that your Google Cloud account and Hugging Face organization are linked. Organizations that already have a credit card on file switch to cloud marketplace billing at the start of their next billing period. Organizations on the free tier with no credit card on file usually switch immediately, so their paid usage is billed through the cloud marketplace right away.

To confirm it, open the billing settings of your organization: the Google Cloud account is now shown as the organization's active payment method.

Congratulations!

Your organization is now billed through your Google Cloud account. All members of your organization can use Hugging Face compute services, and the usage will show up on your Google Cloud bill.

A few things worth knowing:

  • Google Cloud replaces the credit card as the organization's payment method. Usage is metered and reported to Google Cloud, so adding credits is not available while the organization is billed through the marketplace.
  • Included credits still apply: if your organization has a Team or Enterprise subscription, the monthly included credits are applied before any pay-as-you-go usage is reported to Google Cloud.
  • Monitor your usage at any time from the billing section of your organization settings, and find the charges in the Billing reports of the Google Cloud console.
  • Linking and unlinking are audited: both actions are recorded in your organization's audit logs.

Thanks for reading! You can find more details in the billing documentation. If you have any questions, please contact us at billing@huggingface.co.

entries.title: Decision Models in Hugging Face
entries.content:
Update on GitHub

Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.

Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:

"I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today."

The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.

We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.

llama cli -hf ggml-org/gemma-4-e4b-it-GGUF:Q4_0

> We have the following customer support ticket, "I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today.", which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund. Give the answers in JSON.

[Start thinking]
...
[end thinking]
```json
{
  "team_to_handle": "Billing",
  "urgency": "High",
  "request_refund": true
}

But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text?

from transformers import pipeline

decide = pipeline("decision", model="autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide")
decision = decide(
    {
        "state": "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund.",
        "questions": {
            "department": {
                "type": "choice",
                "instructions": "Which team should handle this?",
                "criteria": {
                    "billing": "Payments and refunds",
                    "technical": "Bugs and technical issues",
                    "sales": "Pricing and subscriptions"
                }
            },
        }
    }
)

# {
#   'department': {
#       'type': 'choice',
#       'choice': 'billing',
#       'confidence': 0.9974000453948975,
#       'probabilities': {
#         'billing': 0.9982666969299316,
#         'technical': 0.0010246571619063616,
#         'sales': 0.0007087149424478412
#       }
#     }
# }

This is the key idea behind decision models.

What are decision models?

A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.

TypeSafe AI introduced Jev, describing it as a System One model. The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).

The community has converged to the term decision model, because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". (A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models)

For a decision model, the fundamental interface is:

State + Questions + Allowed Answers → Decisions + Probabilities

Why not use LLMs for everything?

We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.

However, there are a few problems with this approach.

  • LLMs are not guaranteed to follow the requested schema: Even with explicit instructions, a model might produce invalid JSON, introduce unexpected keys, or return an answer outside the allowed choices.
  • Constrained decoding helps, but does not eliminate the computational overhead: Libraries such as Outlines and XGrammar can enforce grammars or JSON schemas by restricting which tokens the model is allowed to generate at each step. This ensures the output follows the supported structural constraints, but introduces additional work.
  • Why generate an entire response: LLMs are designed for open-ended generation, but when our application only needs to choose between predefined answers, autoregressive decoding can be unnecessary work.

How are decision models different from classification models?

Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.

Traditional classification

Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments:

  • Billing
  • Technical support
  • Sales

A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution.

The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head.

If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model.

Zero-shot classification

Zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time.

For example:

from transformers import pipeline

classifier = pipeline(
    "zero-shot-classification",
    model="facebook/bart-large-mnli",
)

classifier(
    "My payment was deducted twice.",
    candidate_labels=["billing", "technical support", "sales"],
)

# {'sequence': 'My payment was deducted twice.',
#  'labels': ['billing', 'sales', 'technical support'],
#  'scores': [0.8466812372207642, 0.0962134450674057, 0.05710534751415253]}

Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs.

from transformers import pipeline

classifier = pipeline(
    "zero-shot-classification",
    model="facebook/bart-large-mnli",
)

classifier(
    "My payment was deducted twice.",
    candidate_labels=["billing", "technical support", "sales", "legal"],
)

# {'sequence': 'My payment was deducted twice.',
#  'labels': ['billing', 'sales', 'technical support', 'legal'],
#  'scores': [0.8185835480690002, 0.09302053600549698, 0.05521026626229286, 0.03318570926785469]}

One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis.

This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is.

Where decision models differ

Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul).

More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions.

Consider these three approaches:

PropertyClassificationZero-shot classificationDecision model
Probability over choicesYesYesYes
Labels defined at inferenceNoYesYes
Multiple typed questionsNoNoYes
Ordered scoring and yes/no decisionsTask-specificPossible with adaptationNative primitives

The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions.

The decision model interface

A decision model request has the following two components:

  • state
  • questions

State

The state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models.

For example:

{
  "customer_message": "I was charged twice. Please refund me today.",
  "subscription": "pro",
  "previous_tickets": 2
}

Questions and their primitives

Questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions:

  • Choice: Select one of several possible answers.
  • Score: Evaluate something on an ordered scale.
  • Noul: Answer a yes/no question probabilistically.

Let's go over them one by one.

Choice: A probability distribution over options

Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification.

Suppose we ask:

Which department should handle this customer request?

The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales.

from transformers import pipeline

decide = pipeline("decision", model="autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide")
decision = decide(
    {
        "state": "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund.",
        "questions": {
            "department": {
                "type": "choice",
                "instructions": "Which team should handle this?",
                "criteria": {
                    "billing": "Payments and refunds",
                    "technical": "Bugs and technical issues",
                    "sales": "Pricing and subscriptions"
                }
            },
        }
    }
)

# {
#   'department': {
#     'type': 'choice',
#     'choice': 'billing',
#     'confidence': 0.9974000453948975,
#     'probabilities': {
#       'billing': 0.9982666969299316,
#       'technical': 0.0010246571619063616,
#       'sales': 0.0007087149424478412
#     }
#   }
# }

The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits ($z_1,\ldots,z_K$), (with K classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax:

Here, (K) is the number of choices.

Consider this illustrative distribution:

ChoiceProbability
Billing0.998
Technical support0.001
Sales0.001

The probabilities sum to one:

The model chooses the option with the largest probability:

In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives.

Score: The expectation of an ordered distribution

Choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale?

Consider the question:

How urgent is this customer request?

We define three levels:

  • 0: Low urgency
  • 1: Medium urgency
  • 2: High urgency
from transformers import pipeline

decide = pipeline("decision", model="autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide")
decision = decide(
    {
        "state": "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund.",
        "questions": {
            "urgency": {
                "type": "score",
                "instructions": "How urgent is the request?",
                "criteria": ["low", "medium", "high"]
            },
        }
    }
)

# {
#   'urgency': {
#     'type': 'score',
#     'score': 1.7053890228271484,
#     'legend': {
#       '0': 'low',
#       '1': 'medium',
#       '2': 'high'
#     },
#     'confidence': 0.5580834252759814,
#     'probabilities': {
#       '0': 0.014908230863511562,
#       '1': 0.26479458808898926,
#       '2': 0.7202972173690796
#     }
#   }
# }

The model again produces a probability distribution:

LevelProbability
0 — Low0.01
1 — Medium0.26
2 — High0.72

Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index.

For a random variable (X) representing the level, the expectation is:

For our example:

The reported score is therefore 

1.7
.

This does not mean that the model selected a fictional level halfway between medium and high. It means that the expectation of its probability distribution is 1.7.

Noul: A Bernoulli decision

The third primitive is Noul, which represents a binary question.

For example:

Is the customer requesting a refund?

from transformers import pipeline

decide = pipeline("decision", model="autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide")
decision = decide(
    {
        "state": "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund.",
        "questions": {
            "refund": {
                "type": "noul",
                "instructions": "Is the customer requesting a refund?"
            }
        }
    }
)

# {
#   'refund': {
#     'type': 'noul',
#     'noul': 0.9947046637535095
#   }
# }

Rather than defining a list of choices, we ask the model to return the probability that the answer is true. We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli).

Let (Y) represent a binary outcome:

where

If the model returns:

{"type": "noul", "noul": 0.92}

it assigns a probability of 

0.92
to Yes and 
0.08
to No.

The model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it.

Confidence: How certain is the model?

So far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called 

confidence
for Choice and Score.

The full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With 

confidence
we achieve just that.

For a Choice with (K) options, the confidence is:

where ($p_{\max}$) is the largest predicted probability.

The intuition here is:

  • A uniform distribution has confidence 0. ($p_{\max} = \frac{1}{K}$). This means the model estimates that all choices are equally likely.
  • A distribution concentrated entirely on one option has confidence 1. ($p_{\max} = 1$)
  • The larger the winning probability relative to a uniform distribution, the higher the confidence.

In our previous three-choice example, Billing had probability 0.80:

Notice that the winning probability is 0.99, but the reported confidence is 0.98. The confidence normalizes the largest probability relative to the number of available options. In contrast, the ordered Score example only had a confidence of 0.558.

Decision models in the Hugging Face ecosystem

Decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations.

Our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common interface without forcing a common implementation. A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once:

  • inference engines like llama.cpp can serve any decision model through the same API
  • the Hub can package and surface them consistently
  • and training tools can target shared primitives instead of individual architectures

The rest of this section walks through each of these pieces.

1. Serving with Transformers

Transformers now supports the 

DecisionPipeline
, 
AutoModelForDecision
, and the 
DecisionConfig
classes. These follow the same overall structure of the pipeline and model classes in 
transformers
but are tailor made for decision models.
from transformers import pipeline

decide = pipeline("decision", model="autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide")
print(decide)

# DecisionPipeline: {'model': 'JevForDecision', 'dtype': 'bfloat16', 'device': 'cuda', 'input_modalities': 'text'}

One can also inspect the configuration and the model like so:

from transformers import AutoModelForDecision, DecisionConfig

model_id = "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide"
config = DecisionConfig.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForDecision.from_pretrained(model_id)

Transformers also supports the 

/v1/systemone
endpoint.

We can start a local server using the serving dependencies:

pip install "transformers[serving]"
transformers serve

Using a compatible version of Transformers, we can then send a decision request:

curl http://localhost:8000/v1/systemone \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide",
    "state": "I was charged twice. Please refund me today.",
    "questions": {
      "department": {
        "type": "choice",
        "instructions": "Which team should handle this?",
        "criteria": {
          "billing": "Payments and refunds",
          "technical": "Bugs and technical issues",
          "sales": "Pricing and subscriptions"
        }
      },
      "urgency": {
        "type": "score",
        "instructions": "How urgent is the request?",
        "criteria": ["low", "medium", "high"]
      },
      "refund": {
        "type": "noul",
        "instructions": "Is the customer requesting a refund?"
      }
    }
  }'

The response contains three named answers with the corresponding typed results and probabilities.

{
  "model":"autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide",
  "answers":{
    "department":{
      "type":"choice",
      "choice":"billing",
      "confidence":0.9974000453948975,
      "probabilities":{
        "billing":0.9982666969299316,
        "technical":0.0010246571619063616,
        "sales":0.0007087149424478412
        }
    },
    "urgency":{
      "type":"score",
      "score":1.7525686174631119,
      "legend":{"0":"low","1":"medium","2":"high"},
      "confidence":0.6288529792800546,
      "probabilities":{
        "0":0.014000383205711842,
        "1":0.2194305807352066,
        "2":0.7665690183639526
      }
    },
    "refund":{
      "type":"noul",
      "noul":0.9953224062919617
    }
  },
  "usage":{"input_tokens":148,"output_tokens":0}
}

An interesting detail is that the above APIs works with compatible autoregressive language models too. Transformers constructs the decision prompts, evaluates the answer label logits in a batched forward pass, and applies softmax without generating response text. This means we can experiment with the decision interface without necessarily training a new model.

2. Serving with llama.cpp

llama.cpp also supports decision models using the same 

/v1/systemone
API.

For example, we can launch a GGUF decision model from the Hub:

llama serve -hf ggml-org/Kev-4B-GGUF

The default server runs on port 9931.

We can then send a request containing the same state and questions, using 

http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone
. With the model selected by the server, we can omit the 
model
field from the request.

The useful property is interface compatibility.

curl http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "ggml-org/Kev-4B-GGUF",
    "state": "I was charged twice. Please refund me today.",
    "questions": {
      "department": {
        "type": "choice",
        "instructions": "Which team should handle this?",
        "criteria": {
          "billing": "Payments and refunds",
          "technical": "Bugs and technical issues",
          "sales": "Pricing and subscriptions"
        }
      },
      "urgency": {
        "type": "score",
        "instructions": "How urgent is the request?",
        "criteria": ["low", "medium", "high"]
      },
      "refund": {
        "type": "noul",
        "instructions": "Is the customer requesting a refund?"
      }
    }
  }'

3. Discovering models on the Hugging Face Hub

Hugging Face introduced a dedicated 

decision-model
tag for discovering compatible models. This is useful because decision models do not have to share a single backbone or architecture.

For example, the ecosystem includes models based on encoder architectures such as ModernBERT, as well as models derived from larger generative language-model backbones.

4. Training decision models using Hugging Face tooling

Once we understand inference, the next question is whether we can adapt a decision model. Since decision models are integrated in transformers, we can fine-tune them with the 

Trainer
API.

Below is a toy example that fine-tunes 

JEV-9B
to route support requests. It is intentionally small, but it shows the parts that matter:
  • each example is a decision request (a 
    state
    plus 
    questions
    ) paired with the gold answer.
  • model.decision_config.prepare_inputs
    turns the request into model inputs, the same way it does at inference time.
  • the model returns one logit per option, so a 
    choice
    question is trained with a plain cross-entropy loss over the options.
import os; os.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"]="2"
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForDecision, Trainer, TrainingArguments

checkpoint = "autotrust/JEV-9B"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(checkpoint)
model = AutoModelForDecision.from_pretrained(checkpoint)

examples = [
    ("I was charged twice. Please refund me.", "refund"),
    ("My package has not arrived.", "shipping"),
    ("The application crashes when I open it.", "technical"),
    ("I want my money back.", "refund"),
    ("Where is my delivery?", "shipping"),
    ("I cannot log into my account.", "technical"),
]

options = {
    "refund": "Billing issues and refunds",
    "shipping": "Orders and deliveries",
    "technical": "Software and account issues",
}

def preprocess(text, label):
    request = {
        "state": text,
        "questions": {
            "category": {
                "type": "choice",
                "instructions": "Classify the support request.",
                "criteria": options,
            }
        },
    }
    (inputs, questions), = model.decision_config.prepare_inputs(
        request, tokenizer
    )
    inputs["marks"] = inputs["marks"].unsqueeze(0)
    inputs["num_options"] = torch.tensor([[len(questions[0].options)]])
    inputs["question_type_ids"] = torch.tensor([[1]])  # choice
    inputs["labels"] = torch.tensor(
        [questions[0].options.index(label)]
    )
    return inputs

dataset = [preprocess(text, label) for text, label in examples]


class DecisionTrainer(Trainer):
    def compute_loss(self, model, inputs, return_outputs=False, **kwargs):
        inputs = inputs.copy()
        labels = inputs.pop("labels")
        logits = model(**inputs)

        logits = logits.unsqueeze(0)  # [3] -> [1, 3]
        loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.float(), labels)

        return (loss, logits) if return_outputs else loss


trainer = DecisionTrainer(
    model=model,
    args=TrainingArguments(
        output_dir="./decision-toy",
        max_steps=30,
        per_device_train_batch_size=1,
        learning_rate=1e-3,
        logging_steps=5,
        save_strategy="no",
        report_to="none",
        remove_unused_columns=False,
    ),
    train_dataset=dataset,
    data_collator=lambda batch: batch[0],
)

trainer.train()

First-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL (huggingface/trl#8040), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open.

If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, Unsloth provides a recipe that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head.

Final thoughts

Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

Traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions.

entries.title: Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan: A Synthetic Dataset Capturing Japan's Demographics and Financial Context
entries.content:
nvidia/Nemotron-PII-Japan

Viewer • Updated • 100k • 111 • 6

Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan: A Synthetic Dataset Capturing Japan's Demographics and Financial Context

Enterprise + Article

A compound AI approach to Japanese personas grounded in real-world distributions

Open Data Breaking Down Privacy Barriers to Pave the Way for AI in Finance

In the financial sector, the utilization of real-world data faces significant constraints due to strict privacy regulations, compliance requirements, and the need for advanced domain expertise. In this context, the development of agentic AI in the financial domain requires synthetic data capable of avoiding the risks of using real data while reflecting demographics, household structures, and asset statuses to reproduce diverse, realistic financial scenarios.

To address these challenges, Elith and NVIDIA have released Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan, a financial domain extension of the open-source persona dataset "Nemotron-Personas-Japan." To our knowledge, it is the first open persona dataset at million-record scale that pairs Japan’s official statistics with household finance and financial literacy data. Built upon official government statistics, this dataset was developed using NeMo SDG-PGMs, a probabilistic graphical model framework for synthetic data generation (SDG), and NeMo Data Designer, an enterprise synthetic data generation system. Furthermore, to enhance the practical utility of the dataset in financial use cases, it was designed by incorporating insights and feedback provided by leading domestic financial institutions and industry associations, including Sompo Japan, Tokio Marine Holdings, Bank of Fukuoka, Mizuho Financial Group, Meiji Yasuda Life Insurance, and the Financial Data Utilization Association (FDUA).

This dataset expands the environment where Japanese developers and enterprises can develop and evaluate AI tailored to local and industry requirements, without using real customer data. Released under the CC BY 4.0 license, it is available for commercial use. From building conversational agents to customer simulation and model evaluation, it supports practical financial AI development. The Nemotron-Personas collection, including Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan, is designed to seamlessly integrate with the user simulation framework NeMo User Sim, enabling instant execution of simulations drawn from diverse distributions consistent with the real world.

What’s in the Dataset?

  • 9M personas total (1M records x 9 personas each), written in natural Japanese
  • 50 fields per record: 9 persona fields, 11 persona attributes, and 30 contextual fields based on official demographic and labor statistics
  • ~1.5B tokens total, including ~750M persona tokens
  • ~950k unique names
  • 1600+ occupation categories reflecting Japan's workforce
  • Comprehensive coverage across demographic, regional, asset distribution, and personality trait axes
  • Diverse persona types: Occupations, sports, arts, travel, cooking, finance, financial behavior, and financial concerns
  • Natural language persona attributes: Cultural background, skills and expertise, career goals and aspirations, hobbies and interests, household/parental/financial background, attitudes toward money, and financial planning
  • Available for both commercial and non-commercial use under the CC BY 4.0 license

How We Built It

Data Generation Pipeline

It was built using NVIDIA’s framework for synthetic data generation, NeMo Data Designer. This compound AI system enables complex Jinja templating, Pydantic validation, structured outputs, automated retries, and support for multiple generation backends. This is the essential toolset required for generating such large-scale synthetic datasets. In addition, the following models were utilized:

  • NeMo SDG-PGMs (Apache-2.0): A probabilistic graphical model framework for statistically grounded data generation
  • gemma-4-31B-it (Apache-2.0): For Japanese text generation

Enhanced Cultural Context

Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan was designed to align with Japan's official demographic and labor statistics while taking into account key considerations essential for AI training:

  • Education: Where national statistics broadly aggregate degree levels, we introduced finer granularity to enable the model to reflect diverse educational pathways.
  • Occupation: We incorporated additional categories (such as business owners and specialized professions) to broaden the spectrum of occupations used for training.
  • Life Stages: We modeled scenarios that rarely surface prominently in statistics, such as students, retirees, and periods of unemployment, to represent more realistic personas.
  • Household Finances: In addition to individual income and spending propensity, we incorporated household-level financial and real assets to replicate diverse economic backgrounds.
  • Digital & Financial Literacy: By including internet and smartphone usage along with financial literacy, we enabled the model to precisely capture consumer profiles in financial use cases.

Private By Design

Every persona is fully synthetic. No real individuals are represented, and the dataset is designed to reduce privacy risk. Demographics and household finances follow official statistics and public survey data, and names follow real Japanese naming patterns. Personas are built from these distributions, not from records about real people.

Who This Data Is For

Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan is built first for teams creating financial AI in Japan, at banks and insurers and at the startups and integrators that serve them. Each persona carries household finances and financial literacy alongside demographics. Teams can use them to build customer-service agents, evaluate sales conversations/marketing initiatives, run user simulations in NeMo User Sim, and red-team customer-facing AI.

The release also serves anyone building for Japanese users. It holds 9M personas, 50% more than Nemotron-Personas-Japan, across 50 fields instead of 22. That gives any Japanese-language project finer slices of the population to train and test on.

Practical AI Applications

The synthetic personas in this dataset can be leveraged for:

  • Multi-turn conversation: Using personas as "seeds" to generate human-like dialogue datasets.
  • Domain-specific AI development: Generating datasets to build AI assistants tailored to realistic scenarios in financial use cases.
  • Bias testing and fairness: Evaluating how models and AI agent systems perform across rural and urban divides, various age groups, educational backgrounds, and economic circumstances to check whether AI performs consistently across Japanese society.

Why It Matters

Access to diverse, high-quality training data that reflects real-world populations has long been a challenge in AI development. Enterprise AI development has predominantly relied on private data, creating barriers for researchers, startups, and particularly AI developers in regions with limited available data.

  • Data Diversity: Reflects the full spectrum of Japan's population, which helps reduce biased training and the risk of model collapse.
  • Cultural Authenticity: Reduces reliance on Western-centric datasets and supports the development of Sovereign AI systems.
  • Privacy and Governance: Aligned with Japan’s innovation-first approach to AI governance. Every persona is synthetic, so no customer data is needed to build or test with it.

By releasing Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan under CC BY 4.0, we provide access to enterprise-grade, high-quality synthetic data, empowering anyone to build culturally grounded AI systems with lower cost and less privacy risk.

Pairs with Nemotron-PII-Japan

Nemotron-PII-Japan launches the same day. It holds 100,000 synthetic Japanese business documents with labeled personal information, for training and testing detection and redaction models. Its documents are built on Nemotron-Personas-Japan. Use Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan to simulate customers, and Nemotron-PII-Japan to test how your pipeline protects their data.

Start Building with Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan

You can download this dataset using the command below to help develop AI that genuinely understands Japanese culture and language.

from datasets import load_dataset
ds = load_dataset("nvidia/Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan")

Use cases for building production-ready applications:

  • Using personas as seeds for dialogue generation
  • Fine-tuning models with culturally grounded data
  • Building personalized engines that reflect Japan's overall demographic makeup
  • Developing domain-specific AI agents equipped with Japanese context

From teams building AI in Japan to global developers aiming for broader regional deployment, Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan dataset provides the authentic, privacy-conscious foundation required for your applications.

entries.title: Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together
entries.content:
Enterprise Article

Higher-Order Pruning of Experts in Mixture-of-Experts Language Models

Introduction

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used.

Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization. Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove.

Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance. Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates.

Our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method.

In this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers.

Experts don't work alone

In a standard MoE, each layer has experts, and each input token is routed independently to such experts ( is a typical choice). Routing is performed by a single layer which produces softmax-normalized gate weights for each expert , wherein the experts with the highest gate weights are selected to form the active set of experts, . The output of the layer is then , where is the output of expert for token .

Left: typical MoE layer, where each token is routed to the top-K experts. Right: first-order methods rank and delete experts based on a scalar importance score, but the best pruning decisions will also consider the strength of interactions between experts.

Importantly, experts in the selected set are not independent. Experts form stable cooperative groups that get consistently co-activated together. This has been observed before in the literature, as well: expert co-selection patterns emerge early in training and stabilize throughout.

This means that when we prune experts from an MoE layer, pruning decisions need to consider the higher-order effects between these experts. Removing expert A might seem fine on its own, but if expert B—which frequently cooperates with and relies on A—is highly important, then removing A would dismantle a cooperative group just through a single deletion. First-order methods miss this entirely, because they score A and B separately.

This effect compounds at high pruning rates. When we remove up to 50% of experts, we risk breaking many cooperative links. This is where second-order pruning is most advantageous.

How HOPE identifies a prune-set

(See Appendix A in our corresponding paper for the full derivation of the HOPE objective)

When we delete a set of experts from some MoE layer, the selected set of experts (for any token ) can change. The pruned experts that would have been selected are replaced by the experts with the next-highest gate weights. The resulting change in layer output is the pruning error. Our goal is to find the prune-set (of some predefined pruning budget ) that minimizes the resulting pruning error (over tokens from our calibration set).

Unfortunately, minimizing the pruning error over directly is intractable. The pruning error depends on the identities of the replacement experts, which in turn depend on the prune-set itself. HOPE sidesteps this by defining a tractable surrogate , which strictly upper-bounds the dominant component of the pruning error:

Because is a squared sum, expanding it naturally produces cross-terms between pairs of experts. These are the interaction terms that first-order methods discard.

To find the optimal prune-set, HOPE minimizes over the calibration set, which can be reformulated as the following quadratic program:

where is defined as:

This F-matrix is collected on the calibration dataset, and the optimal prune-set is obtained by solving the resulting quadratic program (QP) with a continuous relaxation (then rounding to binary solutions). Each entry captures the average gate-weighted output product of experts and , across tokens where both are co-activated. Whereas the diagonal measures individual expert importance, the off-diagonal entries ( for ) measure pairwise cooperative contribution.

What does look like in practice? It shows the structure of expert cooperation, which depends on layer:

Visualization of the interaction matrix F for GLM-4.5-Air (128 experts per layer, 106B parameters total) at three representative layers (early, middle, late). Experts have been clustered to reveal block structure. Bright blocks along the diagonal indicate groups of experts with strong pairwise interaction scores.

In terms of practical cost, HOPE requires the same calibration pass as any other expert-pruning method (one forward pass over calibration data). The only addition is solving the quadratic program, which is non-convex, but can be solved efficiently via a standard QP solver (1–2 seconds each layer). The total additional overhead is negligible compared to first-order methods, as the time for calibration dominates.

Connection to REAP

Notably, HOPE has a strong connection to Router-weighted Expert Activation Pruning (REAP), a state-of-the-art first-order expert-pruning method. HOPE's F-matrix encodes individual expert importance scores on the diagonal, and this diagonal effectively recovers the scores used by REAP to independently rank experts for pruning (differing only by the variance of expert contributions). The diagonal of recovers REAP's expert rankings almost perfectly (Spearman ). Thus, any improvement HOPE achieves over REAP is attributable to the second-order interaction terms in the off-diagonal entries of the -matrix.

Results

We evaluated HOPE as an expert pruning method using 3 models (Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen3.5-35B, and GLM-4.5-Air), with 2 calibration datasets (Evol-CodeAlpaca and SWE-Bench Verified trajectories). We used the Tulu3 suite and SWE-Bench Pro (agentic coding) to test the resulting pruned models, comparing HOPE to 4 first-order baselines (REAP, MAN, EAN, and Frequency) across pruning rates spanning from 10% to 50%.

HOPE achieves the best overall rank across conditions and dominates at aggressive pruning rates. Left: average rank (lower = better) across all models, calibration sets, and benchmarks. Right: SWE-Bench Pro performance on Qwen3.5-35B.

Across all conditions, HOPE achieved the best average rank (2.07 out of 5 methods), with the highest rate of top-1 finishes (39% of conditions) and top-2 finishes (67%). In a head-to-head comparison, HOPE beats every other baseline in the majority of conditions.

As expected, HOPE's advantage grows at higher pruning rates. As more experts are removed, more cooperative links are broken, and the off-diagonal terms of become more important. At 50% pruning, HOPE's average rank improves to 1.58 (vs. 2.42 for the next-best method, REAP). This is also the most deployment-relevant setting, where memory savings are large enough to accommodate longer contexts, deeper reasoning, and more tool calls.

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced on SWE-Bench Pro, an agentic coding benchmark where models must solve real GitHub issues autonomously. These problems involve compositionally diverse tasks (e.g. coding, tool calls, reasoning, etc.) over many turns and likely exercise diverse expert combinations—exactly the regime where preserving cooperative structure matters most. On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 50% pruning, HOPE achieved 42.3 on SWE-Bench Pro, matching the unpruned model's 41.8 (while REAP dropped to 36.2, a 13% regression).

Notably, pruned models can occasionally match or exceed the unpruned baseline, likely because the removal of low-relevance experts reduces noise on the target tasks. This effect is not unique to HOPE and has been observed across pruning methods. Furthermore, our experiments showed that code-focused calibration with any pruning method (including HOPE) did not severely degrade non-coding benchmarks, and HOPE performed well across the Tulu3 suite regardless of calibration set.

HOPE retains more cooperating experts

Average strength of cooperation (measured by F-matrix value) with retained experts, split by experts on which HOPE and REAP disagree.

HOPE's advantage stems from optimizing over the entire interaction matrix . To understand how this affects pruning decisions in practice, we examine the experts where HOPE and REAP disagree. For each disputed expert, we compute its cooperative score (i.e. its average F-value with other retained experts). Experts retained only by HOPE consistently have higher cooperative scores than experts retained only by REAP. In other words, as part of the QP optimization, HOPE sacrifices some individually high-scoring experts in favor of preserving cooperative clusters. The gains in benchmark performance (shown above) validate that this trade-off is advantageous.

How to run HOPE

We created a basic package to run HOPE. It has three steps: 1) calibrate; 2) solve; 3) prune. Our package has been tested on Qwen3, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, and GLM-4.5.

Step 1: Calibrate 

hope calibrate \
    --model-path Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B \
    --prompts calibration_prompts.txt \
    --out-path observations.h5

The calibration step runs a single forward pass over calibration data, whether it be agentic rollouts or single-turn traces. This uses HuggingFace 

transformers
to hook into the forward pass of each individual MoE layer. For each token, this records which experts are selected, their gate weights, output norms, and pairwise co-activation statistics. The output of this step is the F-matrix, stored in an HDF5 file.

Step 2: Solve QP 

hope solve \
    --obs-path observations.h5 \
    --prune-frac 0.50 \
    --out-path pruneset.json

This command materializes the F-matrix and solves the binary quadratic program via a continuous relaxation. This takes a few seconds per layer, and the output is a JSON file which contains the prune-set. This is technically the final output of the HOPE algorithm.

Step 3: Prune 

hope prune \
    --model-path Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B \
    --pruneset-path pruneset.json \
    --out-path ./Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-pruned-50

To complete the pipeline, we run this command to actually create the smaller model checkpoint from the prune-set. The pruned model is a standard HuggingFace checkpoint which is smaller on disk and in memory (no changes to vLLM or SGLang model definitions needed).

We also released a more compact Python API:

from hope.calibrate import calibrate
from hope.solve import solve
from hope.prune import prune_model

calibrate("Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B", calibration_prompts, "observations.h5")
solve("observations.h5", prune_frac=0.50, out_path="pruneset.json")
prune_model("Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B", "pruneset.json", "./Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-pruned-50")

Limitations of HOPE

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced at higher pruning rates (40–50%). At lower pruning rates (10–20%), first-order methods like REAP and MAN are sometimes competitive, and HOPE's advantage shrinks. Additionally, as with most expert-pruning algorithms, HOPE prunes each layer independently and does not account for cross-layer interactions. In our paper, we presented a theoretical framework for cross-layer HOPE, but the results remain preliminary. Finally, HOPE captures pairwise interactions, but even higher-order interactions (triplets and beyond) could provide additional signal, although they are combinatorially difficult to estimate.

More information

For more information, see our corresponding paper and codebase.

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18916

Code: https://github.com/awslabs/HOPE

To see how HOPE can be applied to next-generation hybrid architectures, see our corresponding repository.

    author={Tseng, Alex M. and Kaul, Prannay and Zancato, Luca and Xia, Wei and Soatto, Stefano},
    journal={arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.18916},

entries.title: ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation
entries.content:
allenai/Molmo2-4B-tb

Robotics • Updated • 75 • 1

ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation

Enterprise Article

💻 Code | 📊 Data | 🤖 Models | 📖 Documentation

Robots are learning to fold laundry, sort parts, and handle unfamiliar objects. But those demonstrations are often rather narrow and don't explain what a robot has learned or why it fails.

To study a complex system, scientists often begin with a small, controlled environment, such as a petri dish or terrarium, where they can vary conditions and observe the effects. Robotics needs environments that make this kind of investigation possible—researchers should be able to change the training data or model design, repeat a test, and trace the cause of a failure.

Today we're introducing a framework for creating these environments; we call them FoundationWorlds. Each pairs a controlled, simulated world targeted at studying robotics in a specific environment with tools for automatically generating tasks and training demonstrations, as well as metrics for measuring a robot's behavior over time. Together, they provide a setting for studying questions such as how models improve as more training data becomes available, and how to best combine high-level reasoning with precise physical control.

Our first foundation world is ToyBlocks: an open simulation framework built around a robot arm and blocks on a tabletop. The setting is deliberately simple, but the robot must still reason about how the blocks interact and how to arrange them while pushing, flipping, and stacking.

ToyBlocks automatically generates demonstrations, which are recordings of a robot completing tasks in simulation, without requiring time-consuming teleoperation, in which a person remotely controls the robot. Researchers can easily vary these training experiences. For example, a team could generate more pushing or flipping demonstrations, then evaluate performance on tasks kept out of training.

Starting with ToyBlocks as our first FoundationWorld, we aim to extend the approach to increasingly complex environments.

How ToyBlocks works

Building on our earlier work in open robot learning, including MolmoAct 2, MolmoBot, and MolmoSpaces, ToyBlocks gives researchers a way to study robotics questions in a deliberately constrained domain.

As a FoundationWorld, ToyBlocks is designed around four requirements: (1) realistic physics and appearance, (2) automatic generation of tasks and demonstrations at scale, (3) challenges that combine reasoning with dexterity, and (4) broad coverage of the tasks possible within a domain.

Open-ended domains require modeling a wide range of objects and interactions, making it infeasible to fulfill all these requirements. ToyBlocks’ narrow scope, on the other hand, makes it possible to fulfill them all.

Within ToyBlocks' smaller setting, researchers can work toward investigating how a robot can learn to perform any reasonable task while being confident that the simulated arm and blocks behave very similarly to their physical counterparts.

A physical robot gripper above wooden blocks in the ToyBlocks setup.

ToyBlocks is not just about picking and stacking blocks: pictures and letters on the blocks' faces allow for searching, sorting, and arranging tasks. A robot may need to turn a block to see a hidden face before deciding where it belongs. Domain randomization – varying block size, table height, and other physical properties from scene to scene – tests how well models generalize as the geometry changes.

ToyBlocks automatically generates skills (behaviors for short tasks) and task demonstrations that can be used to train models or adapt previously trained models through additional training (fine-tuning). High-level reasoning models decide what to do; low-level action models control the robot’s movements. The framework can also be used to easily design experiments and validate hypotheses.

ToyBlocks uses reinforcement learning (RL) and motion planning, which computes how the robot should move, to generate skills for short-horizon tasks, which involve brief sequences of actions. Skill training takes place in Isaac Lab, Nvidia's open-source framework for robot learning in simulation. Through trial and error, these policies – models that choose the robot’s actions – learn non-prehensile skills such as pushing a block across the table or flipping it onto another face without picking it up. Skill generation can draw on privileged information – values the simulator can supply directly but a real robot cannot, such as a block's exact position and orientation – instead of estimating it from camera images. This enables the automatic generation of skills that would require teleoperation in the real world.

To generate demonstration data, a task-and-motion planner (TAMP) automatically selects and sequences the skills needed to solve a task and plans the robot’s movements between them. Running each plan in simulation produces a dataset of recorded demonstrations along with labels describing which task or skill the robot performs. ToyBlocks scales data generation through generating and executing hundreds of such plans in parallel on a single graphics processing unit (GPU), reaching up to 24 times real-time performance.

Acting from sensor observations adds a perception problem: a model has to estimate a block’s pose – its position and orientation – which the simulator could supply directly. To reflect real-world conditions, ToyBlocks trains models that map raw sensor observations to actions.

Execution of Molmo 2 (a high-level model) and ManiFlow (a low-level model) trained in ToyBlocks. Molmo 2 selects skills such as rotation and flipping, indicating the relevant block via a pointing interface, while ManiFlow controls the simulated arm to execute the commanded skills.

ToyBlocks' controllable data generator lets users create training mixtures that emphasize particular skills or fill gaps in existing datasets. Researchers can study how much data a model needs and which experiences help it generalize to unseen tasks. For example, they could test whether adding rotation and pick-and-place demonstrations improves flipping, or vary the balance of examples inside and outside a defined workspace region—evaluating their choices on tasks kept out of training. Importantly, evaluation of trained models generates metrics beyond success rates; it provides information such as execution speeds, forces exerted on objects, and task progress measured via the same specifications used by the planning module.

A webpage interface lets users connect Claude – or another frontier model – and use natural language to instruct the robot or try tasks, offering a way to explore how a model plans and acts without needing robotics expertise.

Research building on ToyBlocks

The evaluations below use ToyBlocks to study how training data and methods affect performance, spatial reasoning, generalization to new letters and block appearances, multi-step planning, transfer to physical robots, and frontier models that act through tools. Users can easily design their own tasks and measures to investigate other questions—for example, whether a model performs better when it selects objects by pointing or by issuing text commands such as "pick the yellow block."

Low-level action models: VLA spatial generalization

Low-level action models, such as vision-language-action models (VLAs), map language instructions and visual observations to robot actions.

The premise of VLAs is that, by pretraining on large-scale datasets, they can rapidly generalize to different scenarios or a specific workspace. However, evidence on how well these action models generalize remains conflicting. Some studies report that these action models are brittle to changes in inputs, such as different object layouts and lighting, whereas others show that VLAs generalize well. We argue that these studies often rely on real-world datasets with limited flexibility in spatial variations. ToyBlocks enables us to test how well action models generalize in a simple, easily reproducible setting with meaningful task-space diversity.

We design generalization tests that vary the skill sequences needed to complete an instruction, the letters or colors on the blocks, and the number of blocks in a scene. A stacking study can withhold four-block stacks from training, then test whether a model can combine familiar movements to build them. Workspace studies distinguish performance at new positions within a training region from performance beyond its boundaries, where the model has to extrapolate. We illustrate the study setup and findings below.

We consider four tasks: Stack, Unstack, Flip, and Rotate. For these tasks, we study interpolation (new configurations within the training range) and extrapolation (configurations beyond that range). For example, we evaluate generalization by training on scenarios where objects spawn only in the left region (green) and testing on the right region (orange), or by training on stack heights of 2 and 5 blocks and testing on heights 3 and 4.

Spatial generalization studies for VLA models (results based on ManiFlow, π0.5, and MolmoAct 2). Despite large-scale pretraining, these popular action models generalize poorly in the initial results. We improve generalization and analyze the contribution of each technique. The chart’s LoRA label stands for low-rank adaptation, a method for fine-tuning a model with a small set of trainable weight updates. We believe action model generalization remains far from solved; ToyBlocks provides a valuable testbed for systematically exploring generalization techniques.

High-level reasoning: vision-language models

Long-horizon tasks, which require many steps, allow us to measure how well models can plan a sequence of actions to solve them. Our framework enables us to create such long-horizon tasks, and create oracles – reference components that provide correct plans or actions – at both the high and low levels. This allows us to isolate whether the high-level planning or low-level execution failed when a model fails at a task. An example long-horizon task might be to spell “Ai2” with a block stack; because the letters may not be immediately visible, the agent must first choose actions that reveal information, and then plan and execute a sequence of actions to build the stack.

We evaluate hierarchical models with explicit high-level planning and low-level execution models. In this instance, we choose Molmo 2, a vision-language model (VLM), as the high-level planner, and ManiFlow as the low-level policy. Molmo 2 chooses the skill to execute and the block to execute it on, while the low-level model executes the instruction. We train low-level models such as ManiFlow to pause after completing the execution and query the high-level model for the next instruction. We evaluate the model’s planning abilities on three scenarios of increasing difficulty. The easiest scenario initializes with each character upright and facing the camera. The medium scenario has characters that may not be upright, and the hardest scenario contains characters that are not visible at the start of the episode.

Success rates on three-letter block-spelling tasks using Molmo 2 as the high-level reasoning model and either ManiFlow or a motion planner for low-level manipulation. An example task is “Stack Ai2”. Molmo 2 and ManiFlow are trained on ToyBlocks and evaluated across three difficulty settings and two generalization conditions.

High-level reasoning: agentic systems

Our experiments with agentic systems test how frontier models plan and act through tool calls. We study three settings using Claude Opus 5.5. In the search-and-spell setting, we expose ToyBlocks skills through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standard for connecting AI applications to tools. The agent sees the scene through camera images, calls skills such as pick, flip, or rotate by pointing at a pixel, and decides when to search, build, or declare the task complete or impossible. The same MCP tools can execute either the scripted skills that generate ToyBlocks demonstrations (motion-planned pick and place, plus RL-based rotate and flip) or learned ManiFlow skills. ToyBlocks includes the framework behind these experiments, which also powers the natural-language web interface described earlier.

A frontier model (Claude Fable 5.1) controls a robot in a ToyBlocks world to search for and stack blocks into a tower spelling “Ai2.” During the episode, the agent muses, “I need to figure out whether pick-and-place naturally straightens orientation or if I need to correct it manually… I have 63 calls left, plenty to run a controlled test” (0:06). The agent later hypothesizes: “…maybe the gripper’s yaw is radial—pointing from the robot base toward the block” (0:15) and eventually confirms this hypothesis (0:26) before constructing the three-block tower, but the ‘A’ is sideways (1:11). Surprisingly, current frontier models often make similar perceptual errors (see the next figure), despite their impressive planning, spatial reasoning, and search capabilities.

For classical planning, the agent (our system using Claude Opus 5.5 to plan and choose actions) solves all 30 of a group of block-stacking tasks similar to ones that frontier models struggled with a few years ago, using text descriptions. It also solves 30 out of 30 while repeatedly observing camera images and choosing its next action in a closed loop.

In the search-and-spell setting, the agent had to generate stacks spelling out three-letter words. It had to find the blocks with the corresponding letters among up to eight blocks in the scene. Importantly, 50% of the scenes did not have blocks with all the required letters, rendering the task infeasible. In this case, we required the agent to state that the task is infeasible. We found that in this experiment, the agent was able to successfully solve or correctly declare infeasible 63% of the tasks. Errors were mostly caused by the agent confusing letters with look-alike letters (13%) or choosing an incorrect orientation for a letter in a stack (15%).

Our results also show that the agent was able to solve the task more efficiently when the blocks had semantic regularities, or patterns, taking advantage of such patterns to reason about occluded faces. For instance, in most of the infeasible scenes, when the blocks had no patterns, the agent correctly looked at all the blocks’ faces before declaring infeasibility, whereas it was able to declare infeasibility significantly faster when the blocks had semantic patterns.

Our third experimental setting asks whether an agent can learn how its skills behave, using experiments as a scientist would. When a skill behaves unexpectedly, the agent forms a hypothesis, designs a small test, and revises its understanding from the result. We expand on this idea by having an agent run its own experiments and write its own skill descriptions based on what it finds. These learned descriptions raise success rates from 24% with the default descriptions to 63%, outperforming the 36% achieved with descriptions written by a human expert.

Share of letter-block faces the agent had exposed by the end of each “search and spell” episode (bars averaged over 20 episodes; one marker per episode, styled by outcome). In a feasible task every letter of the three-letter target word is present; in an infeasible task, one letter is missing and the agent should say so. Each patterned block carries uppercase and lowercase instances of a letter, plus images that begin with the letter (e.g., A-block: apple, ant, A, 1, airplane, a); an unpatterned block’s six faces are randomized and unrelated. Correct: the tower spelled the word, or for infeasible tasks, the agent correctly declared the task impossible. Letter rotated or look-alike: the agent built the tower, but a letter was turned or a look-alike substituted, including five infeasible tasks declared solved with a look-alike in the missing letter’s place. Block fell out of reach; reported: a needed block was pushed out of the arm’s reach, so the agent reported that its task had become impossible. No report: the agent used up its motor-skill budget and stopped without claiming either outcome. With patterned blocks, the agent finishes having seen fewer faces, because it can infer what hidden faces must depict rather than checking every one.

Action-conditioned world models as simulators

Action-conditioned world models are trained to predict how a scene changes in response to a robot’s actions. Using them as an alternative to model-based simulators for training and evaluating robot policies is an active area of research. How well they serve this purpose depends on how accurately they predict physical interactions, which is hard to measure without knowing the true state of the scene. ToyBlocks provides this ground truth – the actual simulated scene state – enabling highly controlled tests of how recently developed world models perform in low-level object manipulation. Here, the arm’s end effector is its gripper.

Specifically, we tested whether action-conditioned world models are capable of predicting the motions of blocks or the outcomes of skill executions after being trained on example executions. To do so, we chose four different skills (pick-and-place, flip, rotate, and a mixed task) and generated 900 trajectories – sequences of robot states and actions over time – for each skill. 50% of these trajectories were successful demonstrations of the skill, and 50% were unsuccessful because of small changes to spatial configurations. With equal numbers of successful and unsuccessful executions, a model that always predicts success would be correct only half the time. The models were fine-tuned on these demonstrations and then tested on their ability to predict the outcome of action sequences of the same skills.

We find that Wan 2.2 predicts block motion and task outcomes most accurately. Astra tracks the gripper well but struggles to simulate contact. LeWM is fast and more accurate over short interaction segments, though it drifts over full trajectories. In additional experiments, we also showed that models that score higher on pose and success prediction also produce better training data: adding 100 model-generated trajectories (rollouts) from the best video-generation model raises a policy’s success in an unseen region from 19% to 78%.

We tested three types of models: a video prediction model with 5 billion parameters (Wan 2.2), an agentic model that created its own physics simulator tuned to match the demonstration data (Astra), and a latent world model (LeWM). During testing, each trained model has to predict future images, simulator states, or latent states (learned internal representations), respectively, based on an initial image and a sequence of actions. For full trajectories, models use the initial image as the only observed image, along with the action sequence. For short interaction segments – a single pick, place, flip, or rotate – models start from the real image immediately before that interaction. Full trajectories show how errors accumulate over long horizons, while interaction segments isolate a single interaction, such as the gripper making contact with a block, and show how well the model predicts it. To compare models fairly, we probe each model’s predictions, reading out where it expects the blocks and gripper to be at different points in the trajectory and whether it expects the task to succeed at the end.

Real-world experiments with high- and low-level models

Sim-to-real evaluations test policies trained in simulation on physical robots performing block manipulation tasks. By comparing simulation and real-world execution, we assess whether behaviors and failure patterns observed in simulation provide meaningful indications of real-world performance. For example, researchers can evaluate individual skills and their composition in longer-horizon tasks to identify where failures arise and whether these patterns carry over to physical deployments.

We test whether the models trained entirely on ToyBlocks simulation datasets can be deployed in the real world zero-shot, without training on real-world examples. We evaluate ManiFlow and each low-level skill (pick, place, flip, and rotate) individually. We test whether the hierarchical system (Molmo 2 + ManiFlow) can complete long-horizon three-block spelling tasks requiring sequences of these actions. Real-world experiments use a Franka FR3 arm with a Robotiq gripper across thirty scene configurations. Each scene contains 4–10 blocks seen during training. An episode is successful only if the relevant blocks are moved to target poses without collisions. If the operator intervenes to stop the robot due to an unsafe motion during an episode, it is marked as a failure.

ManiFlow’s atomic-skill success rates were similar in simulation and the real world (80.0% and 81.1%). The hierarchical Molmo 2 + ManiFlow system succeeded in 55.5% of simulated episodes (111/200) and 50.0% of real-world episodes (15/30); further trials are needed to establish statistical confidence across tasks.

Success rates of the ManiFlow low-level model and the hierarchical Molmo 2–ManiFlow system in simulation and the real world. For ManiFlow, the total count represents individual skill executions (pick, place, flip, and rotate), whereas for Molmo 2–ManiFlow, it represents block-spelling task episodes. The Molmo 2–ManiFlow evaluations use the easiest scene configuration defined in the simulation evaluation, with block characters visible and upright.

Side-by-side real-world and simulated block-stacking executions using the same high-level planner. Pink rings mark the planner’s target point for each skill. The scenes use different block labels, and simulation playback is retimed to align grasps and releases with the real robot.

To transfer Molmo 2 and ManiFlow – both trained exclusively on ToyBlocks data – to a physical robot, we address the differences between simulation and reality in three stages.

Before data generation, we perform system identification by tuning simulated robot parameters, including joint friction and armature (the motor and gearbox inertia reflected at the joint), to match real-robot trajectories. During data generation, we randomize physical properties (object size, friction, and table height) and visual properties (lighting, backgrounds, materials, and camera parameters). At inference time, observations are captured using a front-facing ZED camera and a wrist-mounted ZED Mini. For policies that use depth images, we generate clean depth maps, which estimate distance at each pixel, from paired red-green-blue (RGB) camera images using FastFoundationStereo, rather than relying on noisy depth sensor measurements.

The physical ToyBlocks setup: a robot arm, wooden blocks, and a camera.

Opening the tools for further research

ToyBlocks connects data generation, training, and evaluation in one controlled setting, so researchers can investigate how robots learn over time and test how changes to a model or its training data affect robot behavior. We’re releasing simulation assets, procedural task and demonstration generators, automatically generated demonstrations, two trained models showcasing what the framework can do (one based on Molmo 2 and one based on ManiFlow), training code, and evaluation code and validation sets. This allows other teams to build their own training mixtures and investigate failure modes beyond those covered in our initial experiments.

Our initial data release is a proof point with 85,336 long-horizon demonstrations, each comprising about 6–12 skill demonstrations, depending on the set. The initial datasets cover nearly 1,600 hours of robot execution data and 144 million frames. In a few weeks, we're targeting a second release with a larger-scale dataset, more skills, and more comprehensive benchmarking. We’ll also add fully integrated RL training capability that is not contained in the current package.

Other directions for ToyBlocks include bimanual (two-arm) manipulation and dexterous robot hands, equipped with force and touch sensors for studying motion and tasks that involve frequent physical contact. We're also exploring play with unstructured piles of blocks as a way to collect data and study how new behaviors and tasks might emerge through interaction.

Future direction: RL-based pile manipulation.

Future direction: bimanual block manipulation.

With ToyBlocks, we want to advance the science of robot learning toward a future where robots can reliably apply what they've learned to unfamiliar tasks and environments. We encourage the research community to explore ToyBlocks for their own investigations and even as a basis to build their own FoundationWorlds.

Egyptian and Nigerian English join the Open ASR Leaderboard

Update on GitHub

A few months ago, we added private data to the Open ASR Leaderboard: 11 splits from Appen and DataOceanAI covering scripted and conversational speech from five accents (blog). The community response was great, with many highlighting the importance of held-out sets for trustworthy evaluations. Since then, we added one more private split for Indian-accented English with Voice Arena (blog).

We’re excited to announce a new collaboration with Liva AI to add even more private data with two new accents: Egyptian 🇪🇬 and Nigerian 🇳🇬.

DatasetAccentDuration [h]StyleTranscription
Liva AI Conversational EGEgyptian1.34Conversational, spontaneousPunctuated, cased, with disfluencies.
Liva AI Conversational NGNigerian1.55Conversational, spontaneousPunctuated, cased, with disfluencies.

This is part of our continued effort to improve representation in ASR evals (more accents and more languages) and to improve trust (new private data to minimize benchmaxxing, and new data providers). We’re excited to see the community continuing to push ASR performance for the world 🤗

Richer accent breakdown in the Private tab

With these new accents, we can now present a richer breakdown of accents, based on Kachru’s Three Circles (kudos to Hume AI for this idea in their leaderboard). The Open ASR Leaderboard will now report:

  • US vs. non-US (UK, Australia, Canada, India, Nigeria, Egypt)
  • Inner Circle (US, UK, Australia, Canada) vs. Outer & Expanding Circles (India, Nigeria, Egypt)

As more accents join, we’ll split the Outer and Expanding Circles.

About Liva AI

Liva AI collects multimodal interaction data through consumer products used by real people. Because Liva owns both the collection environment and distribution, it can design products around specific model gaps across domains, industries, languages, modalities, and interaction types. This gives it access to natural, high-context behavior that emerges through real product use, rather than artificially elicited or task-based interactions.
